slides.title: Mitigation Methods
slides.teach: These are defensive actions. Learn what each one reduces and when it is the best response to a scenario.

slides.title: Application Allow List
points: Is a safe listing approach for applications
Specifies approved applications that can run
Blocks execution of unauthorized or malicious software
Prevents the execution of unapproved applications

Application Allow List
Is a safe listing approach for applications

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Application allow listing permits only explicitly approved software or code to execute. Everything else is blocked by default.
course.why: It can stop unknown or unauthorized executables even when traditional malware signatures do not recognize them.
course.example: A kiosk can run only the browser and management agent; downloaded executables are denied.
course.exam: Allow list = default deny for unapproved applications. Deny list blocks known bad items but allows unknown ones.

breakdown.term: Is a safe listing approach for applications
breakdown.explanation: Application monitoring measures application behavior, performance, errors, and security events. APM focuses on health/performance, while a WAF inspects and protects web requests.

course.learn: Isolation separates a risky or sensitive system from other resources so compromise cannot easily spread. Physical isolation and air gaps provide stronger separation than ordinary logical controls.
course.why: Reducing connectivity reduces attack paths and lateral movement.
course.example: A malware-analysis workstation is placed on an isolated network with no route to production systems.
course.exam: Air-gapped means no normal network connection. Quarantine is often temporary isolation during an incident.

breakdown.term: Segregates sensitive systems or resources
breakdown.explanation: System monitoring focuses on endpoints and hosts. Endpoint Protection Platforms (EPP) detect or prevent malicious endpoint activity, while SIEM platforms collect and correlate events from many systems.

breakdown.term: Limits the impact of security incidents
breakdown.explanation: This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Mitigation Methods design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.

course.learn: Patching applies vendor fixes that correct vulnerabilities, bugs, or insecure behavior. Effective patch management includes inventory, testing, prioritization, deployment, and verification.
course.why: Known vulnerabilities remain easy targets when fixes exist but are not deployed.
course.example: A critical Internet-facing server receives an emergency security update after testing confirms application compatibility.
course.exam: If an official fix exists, patching is usually the direct remediation—unless operational constraints require a compensating control first.

breakdown.term: Ensures the security of the enterprise IT infrastructure
breakdown.explanation: Infrastructure monitoring observes networks, cloud configuration, appliances, links, and supporting resources. NSM analyzes network behavior, while CSPM evaluates cloud security posture and misconfiguration.

defs: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.
Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.

course.learn: Encryption converts plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand the data. Symmetric encryption uses a shared secret; asymmetric encryption uses a public/private key pair.
course.why: Encryption is one of the primary ways to protect confidentiality for data at rest and in transit.
course.example: A laptop uses full-disk encryption, while a TLS session protects web traffic crossing an untrusted network.
course.exam: Encryption = confidentiality and reversible with the correct key. Hashing is one-way and primarily supports integrity.

course.learn: Security monitoring continuously observes systems, networks, applications, and logs for suspicious activity, failures, policy violations, and indicators of compromise.
course.why: Early detection shortens attacker dwell time and gives defenders evidence for response.
course.example: Endpoint and network telemetry reveal an unusual process making outbound connections immediately after a phishing attachment opens.
course.exam: Monitoring is detective; it should feed alerting, investigation, containment, and validation.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Granting only the minimum permissions required to perform a task.

course.learn: Least privilege gives users, applications, and services only the permissions required for their legitimate tasks and no more.
course.why: If an account is compromised, limited privilege reduces what the attacker can access or change.
course.example: A backup service account can read required data and write to the backup repository but cannot log on interactively as an administrator.
course.exam: Minimum necessary permissions = least privilege. Just-in-time access can reduce standing privilege even further.

breakdown.explanation: This concerns who or what can reach a resource and what actions are permitted once access is granted.

breakdown.explanation: This affects the likelihood or impact of harm and therefore changes how the organization should prioritize controls.

Prevents misconfigurations that may lead to vulnerabilities

slides.raw:
Configuration Enforcement

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Configuration enforcement keeps systems aligned with an approved secure baseline and detects or corrects drift from required settings.
course.why: One insecure change can reopen a vulnerability even after a system was originally hardened.
course.example: A device-management platform automatically re-enables the host firewall if a local user disables it.
course.exam: Baseline + continuous enforcement/drift correction are the clues.

breakdown.term: Ensures systems and devices adhere to secure configurations
breakdown.explanation: System monitoring focuses on endpoints and hosts. Endpoint Protection Platforms (EPP) detect or prevent malicious endpoint activity, while SIEM platforms collect and correlate events from many systems.

breakdown.term: Prevents misconfigurations that may lead to vulnerabilities
breakdown.explanation: Misconfiguration means a system is deployed with unsafe settings such as default credentials, unnecessary services, open permissions, exposed management interfaces, or insecure cloud access.

breakdown.term: Enhances consistency in security settings
breakdown.explanation: This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Mitigation Methods design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.

breakdown.term: Strengthens the overall security posture of the organization

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Decommissioning safely removes a system or service from use by revoking access, removing network exposure, handling data, updating inventory, and disposing or repurposing the asset securely.
course.why: Forgotten systems become unmanaged attack surface and retired storage can leak data.
course.example: Before recycling a server, the organization removes credentials, wipes or destroys drives, removes DNS/firewall entries, and updates the asset inventory.
course.exam: Retire securely—not simply power off and forget.
